text:
Recent work supports separating persistent taste from immediate intent. [MSMT-LSI (2024)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-024-00460-5) uses temporal embeddings and separate long-/short-history attention networks, then combines their representations. [Elastic Multi-intent Adaptation (2024)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10400839/) explicitly retains existing intents, detects new ones, and removes inactive intents under memory constraints. These approaches challenge a single fixed sequence summary, although neither establishes that inferred interests correspond to identifiable purchase motivations.

[HyperHawkes (WWW 2025)](https://evazangerle.at/publication/peintner-www-2025/) is especially relevant: session hypergraphs and contrastive clustering infer latent intents; Hawkes processes model recurring intent and long-term interests; a multi-level attention mixture captures short-term changes. Its alternating optimization and graph machinery add complexity. A lightweight hypothesis inspired by these results: retain SASRec, add pooled long-history and recent-window representations, and learn a gate conditioned on recent events and observed time gaps. Multiple decay scales or a small bank of latent-interest vectors could represent switching without explicit intent labels. This simplification is a proposed experiment, not a published performance claim.

Text-based intent methods need careful filtering. [IntentRec (2025)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S156742232500047X) relies on review text and pretrained BERT, making it unsuitable here. A compliant alternative worth testing is a randomly initialized token-embedding pool over available titles/descriptions, jointly trained with next-item prediction and fused with item IDs. Treat text similarity, complementarity, recurring needs, and fulfilled needs as hypotheses; interactions and timestamps do not directly label them. Compare additions through the common macro validation HR@10 across all four categories.
